build_hypa(): which paths are anomalous

honets

2026-08-26

The analytic question

A frequent path is not necessarily a surprising one. Specify -> Command is common largely because Specify and Command are both common — the count tells you about the states, not about the pairing.

build_hypa() (LaRock et al. 2020) separates the two. It asks: given how often each state is entered and left, how often would this path occur by chance? The null is a Wallenius non-central hypergeometric model, which holds the marginal in- and out-degrees fixed and lets the paths fall where they may. A path that beats its own expectation is carrying information the degree structure does not explain.

library(honets)
seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
library(cograph)

Running it

hp <- build_hypa(seqs, order = 2)
hp
HYPA: Path Anomaly Detection
  Order(s):     2
  Edges:        702
  Anomalous:    185 (alpha=0.05, p_adjust=BH)
    Over-repr:  139
    Under-repr: 46

Of the 702 second-order paths, 139 occur significantly more often than expected and 46 significantly less, after Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

The top row occurs 10.3 times more often than the degree structure predicts. That is the signature of a routine — a sequence the sessions actually follow, rather than one the marginals happen to produce.

  p_adjusted_under p_adjusted_over order
1     1.148020e-02               1     2

3     4.492428e-02               1     2
4     3.294294e-05               1     2

Specify -> Specify -> Command is observed 77 times against an expectation of 126 — a ratio of 0.61. It is a frequent path (77 occurrences is not rare) that is nonetheless avoided. A count-based analysis would list it among the common transitions and miss entirely that it happens far less than it should.

Absences are hard to see and easy to under-report. This is the column that finds them.

Seeing the anomalies

plot_simplicial() dispatches on net_hypa and ranks pathways by ratio, so the most extreme deviations come first. dismantled = TRUE gives each path its own panel, which is what makes overlapping routines readable.

plot_simplicial(hp, anomaly = "over", max_pathways = 9,
                dismantled = TRUE, ncol = 3)

The under-represented half — the paths the sessions avoid — is the harder one to see in a table and the easier one to see here:

plot_simplicial(hp, anomaly = "under", max_pathways = 6,
                dismantled = TRUE, ncol = 3)

The most surprising paths and the most frequent surprising paths are different sets. Sort by ratio to find structure; sort by observed to find structure that carries weight. Report which you used.

Multiplicity is handled, and directional

702 paths are tested, so raw p-values would be meaningless. build_hypa() applies Benjamini-Hochberg by default and reports separate adjusted values for each direction — p_adjusted_over and p_adjusted_under — because a path cannot be simultaneously over- and under-represented and pooling them would be wrong.

as.data.frame(hp, sort_by = "p", top = 4)
                             path               from        to observed
1 Specify -> Specify -> Interrupt Specify -> Specify Interrupt       34
2   Specify -> Command -> Command Specify -> Command   Command       98
3  Refine -> Specify -> Interrupt  Refine -> Specify Interrupt       31
4   Command -> Specify -> Specify Command -> Specify   Specify       77
  expected     ratio      p_value      p_under p_over anomaly p_adjusted_under
1 149.6387 0.2272139 1.972657e-30 1.972657e-30      1   under     1.384805e-27
2 233.7660 0.4192226 2.830720e-24 2.830720e-24      1   under     9.935826e-22
3 111.4193 0.2782282 1.378800e-19 1.378800e-19      1   under     3.226391e-17
4 179.8758 0.4280733 2.219127e-18 2.219127e-18      1   under     3.894568e-16
  p_adjusted_over order
1               1     2
2               1     2
3               1     2
4               1     2

p_value is the two-sided value; the directional adjusted columns are the ones to act on. alpha and p_adjust control the threshold and method:

hp_strict <- build_hypa(seqs, order = 2, alpha = 0.001, p_adjust = "bonferroni")
hp_strict
HYPA: Path Anomaly Detection
  Order(s):     2
  Edges:        702
  Anomalous:    42 (alpha=0.00, p_adjust=bonferroni)
    Over-repr:  15
    Under-repr: 27

Under Bonferroni at α = 0.001 the anomaly count falls sharply — the paths that survive are the ones worth naming in a result.

min_count and order

do.call(rbind, lapply(c(5, 20), function(mc) {
  h <- build_hypa(seqs, order = 2, min_count = mc)
  data.frame(min_count = mc, scored = nrow(as.data.frame(h)),
             over = h$n_over, under = h$n_under)
}))
  min_count scored over under
1         5    702  139    46
2        20    702   53    35

Higher orders test longer paths, and the table grows quickly — check that each path still has enough observations to support a claim.

What to do next

  • build_hon() — HYPA scores paths against a null; BuildHON+ decides which contexts deserve their own node. They answer different questions about the same sequences.
  • bootstrap_hon() — resampling-based stability for extracted rules.
  • path_dependence() — per-context divergence rather than per-path anomaly.
  • pathways() — pass the scored paths on to the simplicial family.

References

  • LaRock, T., Nanumyan, V., Scholtes, I., Casiraghi, G., Eliassi-Rad, T., & Schweitzer, F. (2020). HYPA: Efficient detection of path anomalies in time series over networks. Proceedings of the 2020 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining, 460-468.
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 57(1), 289-300.
